title: Multi-armed Bandits
oneLiner: The simplest RL problem: pick among a few slot machines again and again, and learn which pays best without wasting too many pulls finding out.

what.html:
A k-armed bandit is a row of k slot machines ("arms"), each paying random rewards around its own hidden average. You get many pulls. To win the most you must keep an estimate of each arm's average and decide each time: pull the arm that looks best (exploit), or try another to learn more (explore).

Everyday versionChoosing a lunch place: go back to your current favourite, or try the new place that might be even better? Only ever going to the favourite means you might never discover the best one.

why.html:
• Online ads, A/B tests and recommendations are bandit problems.
  • It isolates the exploration–exploitation dilemma that appears in all of RL.
  • The tools (running averages, ε-greedy, UCB, softmax with a baseline) are reused all the way to deep RL.

how.title: Each arm has a true value
how.html: Every arm has a hidden expected reward q*(a). We estimate it with Q(a). Picking the arm with the biggest Q is exploiting; anything else is exploring.

how.title: Average what you've seen, then be greedy?
how.html: Estimate each arm by the average of its rewards so far. Always picking the best-looking arm (greedy) is risky: an unlucky first pull can make the truly best arm look bad, and greedy never goes back to check.

how.title: ε-greedy: explore a little
how.html: Most of the time pick the best-looking arm; with a small probability ε pick any arm at random. With two arms and ε = 0.5 the greedy arm is still picked 75% of the time (50% on purpose + half of the random 50%).

how.title: A fair race: the testbed
how.html: To compare strategies, run them on thousands of random 10-armed problems and average. Greedy stalls at about 35% best-arm picks; ε = 0.1 reaches about 81%.

how.title: Running averages
how.html: No need to store every reward: new estimate = old + (1/n) × (reward − old). Rewards 10, 0, 8 give estimates 10, 5, 6.

how.title: When arms change over time
how.html: If an arm's payout drifts, use a fixed step α instead of 1/n so recent rewards count more. Old rewards fade exponentially: with α = 0.5 the last reward gets weight 0.5, the one before 0.25, and so on.

how.title: Optimism as exploration
how.html: Start every estimate unrealistically high (say +5). Each arm disappoints when tried, so a purely greedy agent still ends up trying them all. It only helps at the start.

how.title: UCB: explore what's uncertain
how.html: Add a bonus to each arm's estimate that's big when the arm has rarely been tried. Pick the highest "estimate + bonus". Exploration goes to promising-but-uncertain arms, not random ones.

how.title: Learn preferences directly
how.html: Instead of values, keep a preference per arm and turn them into probabilities with a softmax. If a pull beats the running average reward, make that arm more likely; if not, less likely. This is the seed of policy-gradient methods.

demo.html: You get 40 pulls on five machines. Try to finish with the highest total, then let ε-greedy play and compare. Reveal the true means at the end to see how much you "regretted".

example.html:
Spot the exploration. Four arms, all estimates start at 0. Pulls: arm 1 pays 1; arm 2 pays 1; arm 2 pays 2; arm 2 pays 2; arm 3 pays 0. At step 2 arm 1 was the clear leader but arm 2 was chosen, so that was definitely a random exploration. At step 5 arm 2 led (about 1.67) but arm 3 was chosen: exploration again. Steps 1, 3 and 4 could have been greedy (or random picks that happened to match).

Supplementary Constant-step-size estimates never completely forget the starting guess: with α = 0.5 after four rewards the start still carries weight 0.0625.

misunderstandings: Greedy is optimal once you have estimates.
Early luck can trap greedy on a worse arm.
The random pick can land on the greedy arm too.
Constant α gives an unbiased average.
It keeps a fading bias from the initial guess.
The push to explore fades after the first tries.
takeaways: Bandit = one situation, many actions, noisy rewards.
Estimate values by (incremental) averages; greedy can get stuck.
ε-greedy, optimistic starts and UCB are ways to explore.
Constant α tracks changing arms with recency weighting.
Gradient bandits learn a softmax policy with a reward baseline.
thirty: A k-armed bandit repeatedly offers k actions with unknown expected rewards q*(a). Sample-average estimates Qₜ(a) can be updated incrementally, Qₙ₊₁ = Qₙ + (1/n)(Rₙ − Qₙ), or with a constant α for nonstationary problems, giving an exponential recency-weighted average that keeps a fading bias from Q₁. Greedy selection can lock onto a suboptimal arm; ε-greedy explores randomly (with k = 2 and ε = 0.5 the greedy arm is still chosen 75% of the time). On the 10-armed testbed ε = 0.1 reaches about 81% optimal actions vs about 35% for greedy. Optimistic initial values force early exploration in stationary problems; UCB adds an uncertainty bonus c√(ln t/N(a)); gradient bandits learn softmax preferences with a reward baseline, previewing policy-gradient methods.
